dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — Benji is four days old, and Mike, you're off work today to help Kelly at home, which is exactly where the day should be spent. Overnight, the Ukraine aid-centre death toll rose to 42 ahead of next week's Abu Dhabi peace talks, oil fell for a fourth straight day on hopes the midterm result pushes Washington toward an Iran deal, and the post-election map settled: Democrats hold both chambers of Congress, and Ohio has a governor-elect in Amy Acton and a returning senator in Sherrod Brown. The Cavs lost the rematch in Oklahoma City last night, 124-116, despite Donovan Mitchell's late flurry, and Jarrett Allen left early with a knee knock — they're home Friday against Philadelphia and Saturday against the Knicks. Solon stays cloudy and dry today with a high near 61°, but rain and a sharp cooldown arrive Friday into Saturday, so today is the day for any errands. If energy somehow allows tonight, Hadestown is at Playhouse Square at 7:30 PM.

weekBrief.text: Benji's first full week at home is a settle-in week: he was born Sunday, came home Tuesday, saw his pediatrician Wednesday, and now gets a quiet house while Mike takes Thursday off to help Kelly. Solon's weather turns with the weekend — cloudy and dry near 61° Thursday, then rain and a sharp cooldown Friday (49°) and Saturday (46°), clearing Sunday and rebounding into the 50s and low 60s through Tuesday. The week's best grocery move is a Thanksgiving stock-up: Meijer brand frozen turkeys at 79¢/lb or less through November 26 beat Giant Eagle's 95¢/lb, and one bird covers a roast dinner now plus soup and chili later. If energy allows, the Cavs are home twice at Rocket Arena — Friday against Philadelphia and Saturday against the Knicks — alongside Hadestown at Playhouse Square on Thursday, the free Día de Muertos celebration on Saturday, Ohio State hosting Oregon Saturday afternoon, and the Browns at New Orleans on Sunday.

Ukraine aid-centre death toll rises to 43 as rescue work enters a fourth day
items.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday that 43 people have now been confirmed killed in Monday's Russian bombing of a school building in Komyshuvakha, in the Zaporizhzhia region. The building was being used as a shelter and as a place where residents gathered to receive humanitarian aid, and more than 30 people were still unaccounted for.

Local officials said at least nine heavy aerial bombs hit the site, including very large glide bombs that collapsed a reinforced underground shelter built to protect people during attacks. Two first responders who rushed in after the first strikes were among those killed, and identification of many victims is expected to require DNA testing because of the scale of the damage.

The Council of Europe's human rights commissioner condemned the attack, noting that the aid distribution had been publicly announced. It is being described as one of the deadliest single attacks on civilians in the war, coming just days before planned peace talks.

Watch for the final toll as crews clear the rubble, and for how the attack is raised at the Abu Dhabi talks scheduled for November 10-11.

items.title: Tankers burn near the Strait of Hormuz as Iran reports mine strikes and a ship is hit off Qatar
items.summary:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Thursday that two oil tankers and a tugboat caught fire in separate incidents in the Strait of Hormuz after using routes Tehran calls unauthorised. One tanker was said to have struck a naval mine south of the strait, while a supertanker caught fire leaving the waterway and a tug that came to help it also burned.

The report follows a claim a day earlier that four tankers were destroyed after hitting mines and two other vessels were seized. Separately, Britain's maritime trade operations agency said it had received a report of a tanker struck by two unidentified projectiles north of Qatar, with the crew's status not yet confirmed.

Hormuz is the main exit route for Gulf oil, so repeated mine and fire incidents raise shipping, insurance and supply risks at a moment when crude had been falling on hopes of an Iran deal and then rebounded on Thursday. Iran gave no casualty or damage figures, and independent confirmation is still limited.

Watch for confirmation from shipping agencies, whether tanker companies pause transits, and how oil prices react into Friday.

items.title: Bank of England raises rates to 4% for the first time since 2023 and warns more may come
items.summary:
The Bank of England raised its main interest rate to 4% from 3.75% on Thursday, its first increase in more than three years. The vote was 8 to 1, and the lone dissenter wanted an even bigger move to 4.25%, arguing the bank had been too slow to reassure markets about inflation.

British inflation was 3.5% in September, and the bank now expects it to peak near 4.8% next spring and not return to its 2% target until late 2028, about six months later than it forecast in July. In a worse case, with oil around $130 a barrel, inflation could reach above 6% next year. Growth forecasts were revised up, helped by spending on artificial intelligence.

Governor Andrew Bailey said this should not be read as the start of an endless run of hikes, but that unless the Middle East conflict settles, it is unlikely to be the last one either. That adds a direct cost-of-living pressure for Britain's new government, with real household incomes set to fall this year and next.

The next decision comes on December 17. Watch whether support grows for larger hikes, and how markets price the path for 2027.

items.title: Ukraine expects fresh support after the U.S. midterms, its foreign minister says
items.summary:
Ukraine's foreign minister Andrii Sybiha said on Thursday that he expects new steps to support Ukraine following the U.S. midterm elections. Speaking at a press conference in Bucharest, he said every change brings a chance for new dynamics.

Sybiha said it is not realistic to end the war with Russia without the United States and President Donald Trump, but argued that Europe needs a clearer complementary role alongside the main U.S. track. He also said Ukraine does not see signs on the battlefield that Russia is ready for serious negotiations, and that pressure on Moscow needs to continue.

The comments came ahead of negotiations involving Ukraine, Russia and the United States in Abu Dhabi next week. Ukraine says it will use any opportunity to speed up peace efforts.

Watch for what the new Democratic Congress proposes on Ukraine aid, and whether Europe announces concrete new commitments before Abu Dhabi.

items.title: Zelensky appeals in Madrid for transformers, cables and generators to keep Ukraine's power on
items.summary:
President Volodymyr Zelensky appealed on Thursday to leaders at the Ibero-American Summit in Madrid for urgent help rebuilding and maintaining Ukraine's war-damaged energy system. He asked for transformers, cables, generators and other electrical equipment.

Zelensky said Russia had damaged every power plant in the country through missile and drone attacks, forcing energy workers into constant repairs to prevent a nationwide blackout. He named specific needs by country, including transformers from Brazil, Mexico, Argentina and Colombia, cables from Chile, and equipment and generators from Spain.

He also used the summit to call for pressure over Russian war crimes, citing the school aid-centre attack, and to invite cooperation on defence technology, including drones, electronic warfare and air defences. Spain's prime minister said Ukraine deserved support.

Watch for pledges that turn into deliveries before winter, when power shortages bite hardest.

items.title: Germany proposes an extra 100 million euros to repair Ukraine's water, energy and transport links
items.summary:
Germany is proposing to set aside an extra 100 million euros, about $113 million, to help restore Ukrainian water, energy and transport infrastructure and make it more resilient against intensified Russian attacks, according to a finance ministry letter to parliament's budget committee.

The money would supplement funding already in the 2026 budget and cover damage from a Russian aerial campaign that has intensified since the summer. Berlin had already set aside 250 million euros in September through the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.

The letter said 80% of Ukraine's power generation capacity has been destroyed since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, with October attacks creating blackouts in more than a third of Ukraine's regions. Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government is described as the biggest European contributor to Ukraine.

Watch for the budget committee's decision, and whether other European governments add similar winter infrastructure packages.

items.title: Democrats won big, but they are already split over what their mandate actually is
items.summary:
Democrats are presenting their sweeping midterm victory as a mandate for change, but reporting on Thursday showed early disagreement inside the party over how far voters want them to go. There is broad agreement on affordability, and less agreement on investigations, impeachment, or moving toward government-run health coverage.

Leaders Chuck Schumer and Hakeem Jeffries have stressed that fixing the affordability crisis is the top priority. The consensus list for January includes making Obamacare plans more affordable, reversing some Medicaid cuts, and ending the tariffs and the war in Iran that Democrats blame for higher costs.

Schumer warned that voters did not give Democrats a blank check. Jeffries said he has not had a single House Democrat talk to him about impeachment, even as other members push for tougher accountability for President Trump and his family.

Watch for the first bills Democrats file in January, and whether centrists and progressives can hold together on health care.

items.title: Democrats promised affordability, but Trump's veto and the filibuster limit what they can deliver
items.summary:
Democrats swept to power in Congress promising to lower prices for groceries, gasoline, health care and other necessities, but Axios reporting on Thursday laid out how limited their power is to deliver that relief on their own. The biggest obstacle is President Trump, who retains the veto.

Economists noted that slowing inflation does not mean prices fall back to earlier levels, and that broad price declines usually come with downturns and job losses. One budget expert told Axios that bringing prices back to 2019 levels is not realistic.

Democrats campaigned on rolling back tariffs, suspending the federal gasoline tax in some proposals, offering rebate checks, restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies and reversing Medicaid cuts. Each of those paths runs into a veto threat, the Senate's 60-vote threshold, or divisions inside the party.

Watch for whether Democrats use spending and borrowing bills as leverage to negotiate, rather than relying on standalone bills Trump can block.

items.title: Democrats vow to rein in Trump after winning both chambers, as Trump points to his veto
items.summary:
Democrats vowed to use their midterm victory to rein in President Donald Trump, setting up two years of possible deadlock in Washington. A wave of anger over Trump's policies, particularly the war with Iran and its effect on living costs, helped Democrats take the Senate with at least a 54-44 majority and gain at least 30 House seats.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said the incoming majority would focus on affordability and accountability, and that the House would no longer function as a subsidiary of the Trump administration. Trump, appearing at the construction site for his White House ballroom, said he would probably get along with Democrats unless they wanted to be destructive, but stressed that he has the power of the veto.

Two very close Senate races, in Alaska and Mississippi, remained uncalled, leaving open the possibility that the Democratic majority could grow to 56-44.

Watch for how Democrats use investigations and nominee confirmations, where the Senate majority gives them real blocking power even without Trump's signature.

items.title: Vance says the Iran war cost Republicans the midterms
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance blamed the Iran war for Republican midterm losses, in remarks reported after the party lost both chambers of Congress. The comment was a notable public break in how the administration explained a result that Democrats tied to the war and to higher living costs.

Republicans are debating whether the defeat was mainly about the war, about tariffs and prices, or about President Trump's broader standing. Vance's framing puts foreign policy at the centre of that argument, rather than treating the loss as only a domestic economic verdict.

The remark matters because the new Democratic Congress has promised to use funding bills to impose limits on the administration and on the war in Iran. If senior Republicans also see the war as a political liability, pressure for a settlement could grow inside both parties.

Watch for whether Trump adopts Vance's explanation, and for Republican calls to change course in the coming days.

items.title: Speaker Mike Johnson steps aside as Scalise and Jim Jordan vie to lead House Republicans
items.summary:
House Speaker Mike Johnson will not seek to stay on as his party's leader after Democrats erased the Republican majority, according to reporting this week. His decision opens a leadership race in a House Republican conference reeling from the midterm result.

Majority Leader Steve Scalise and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan are the two names most often floated as successors, reviving a contest between figures who also figured in the party's 2023 leadership fights. Johnson had previously told interviewers he expected to remain the top Republican regardless of the outcome.

The winner will lead a smaller Republican minority that still holds a key weapon: Democrats do not have the two-thirds majorities needed to override a presidential veto on their own, so Republican votes will matter on any bill meant to become law over Trump's objections.

Watch for the timing of the leadership vote, and whether the race becomes a proxy fight over how closely House Republicans stay aligned with Trump.

items.title: Nasdaq falls 5.52% into correction in Wall Street's worst day since April 2025
items.summary:
The Nasdaq Composite dropped 5.52% on Thursday to close at 24,315, entering correction territory, while the S&P 500 fell 4.36% to about 7,354 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average plunged 3.44%, losing about 1,833 points. All three indexes had their worst session since April 2025, erasing the rally that followed the midterm results.

Semiconductors were hit hardest. The Philadelphia chip index fell about 12%, with SanDisk down more than 20% and Micron, AMD and Marvell each down around 17%, while Nvidia fell about 9%. Data-centre operators also fell sharply, and Tesla and other large tech names lost ground.

Investors tied the selloff to a reassessment of the artificial intelligence trade after Democrats won Congress, amid worries that closer scrutiny of data-centre buildout could slow AI spending. Reuters estimated about $2 trillion was wiped off the Nasdaq's market value on the day.

Friday's October jobs report is the next test. Watch whether the selloff spreads beyond tech, and how the Federal Reserve rate outlook shifts.

items.title: Chip stocks plunge 7% or more in early trading as Qualcomm's miss sparks a broader tech slump
items.summary:
U.S. stocks dropped sharply on Thursday morning, with the Nasdaq on course for correction territory as steep losses in chip and data-centre stocks weighed a day after the midterm result powered a broad rally. Qualcomm slid about 9% after its smartphone chip sales fell short of Wall Street estimates.

The broader semiconductor index extended declines and was down 7.1% in morning trading, with losses in Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Intel and Marvell. Data-centre operators IREN, Hut 8 and Applied Digital fell between 6% and 11%, and Meta, Amazon and Alphabet also lost ground, while Tesla tumbled.

At 9:57 a.m. ET the Dow was down 352 points, or 0.66%, the S&P 500 was down 1.66%, and the Nasdaq was down 3.09%. Those morning losses deepened into the close.

The morning move set the tone for the day: a company-specific miss at Qualcomm became a sector-wide question about phone demand and about how much AI spending is already priced in.

items.title: Qualcomm falls sharply as smartphone chip sales miss forecasts
items.summary:
Qualcomm shares fell sharply after the chipmaker reported weaker-than-expected smartphone chip sales, with handset revenue down 26% year over year to about $5.14 billion, below the roughly $5.25 billion analysts expected. Total quarterly revenue fell 8% to about $10.3 billion.

At least eight brokerages cut their price targets after the report, according to market data cited in coverage of the results. The miss overshadowed momentum in Qualcomm's data-centre business, which investors had been watching as a growth story.

Because Qualcomm is a bellwether for phone demand, the result fed a broader worry on Thursday that consumer device demand is softening at the same time AI infrastructure stocks are being repriced.

Watch for guidance from other handset suppliers, and whether Qualcomm's data-centre growth can offset phone weakness in coming quarters.

items.title: Reuters calls Thursday a market bonfire as the AI trade implodes
items.summary:
Reuters' Trading Day wrap described Thursday as a bonfire for U.S. stocks, led by a ferocious selloff in tech and AI-related shares as investors reassessed what the Democrats' sweeping midterm wins mean for the AI data-centre buildout. Chip stocks posted their second-biggest fall on record.

The wrap put the closing moves at Nasdaq down 5.5%, S&P 500 down 4.4% and Dow down 3.4%, with all 11 S&P sectors falling, tech down 7.3%, and the Philadelphia chip index down 12%. Bitcoin fell about 6% to around $75,000, and rate traders pushed back the expected timing of the Federal Reserve's next hike to March.

Reuters noted the Nasdaq is now firmly in correction territory, down as much as 14% from its all-time high reached only a month ago.

Watch for Friday's employment data, with economists expecting about a 65,000 rise in October non-farm payrolls and unemployment holding at 4.2%.

items.title: Why the blue wave turned Wall Street red: data-centre worries hit AI stocks
items.summary:
Thursday's selloff was tied directly in market coverage to the midterm result, as investors worried that a Democratic Congress will slow development of data centres and artificial intelligence projects. The Nasdaq closed down 5.52%, the S&P 500 down 4.36%, and the Dow down 3.44%.

Double-digit percentage losers included Advanced Micro Devices, SanDisk, Micron, Dell and Marvell Technology. The moves reversed Wednesday's post-election gains and left the Nasdaq more than 10% below its high from last month.

Analysts quoted in coverage said entering correction territory does not by itself end the AI trade, but it may signal that investors will be more selective about which AI names they own and what they will pay for growth.

Watch for company-level differentiation in coming sessions, rather than a single AI basket moving together.

items.title: AMD posts a record quarter as data-centre sales nearly double, even as its shares get swept into the selloff
items.summary:
AMD reported a record $13.4 billion quarter, with data-centre sales nearly doubling, in results that underlined how strong underlying demand for AI computing hardware has been. The numbers landed in a week when AMD's shares were nevertheless swept into a broad semiconductor selloff.

The contrast is the story of Thursday in miniature: company results pointing to continued AI spending, and a market suddenly unwilling to pay previous prices for that growth after the political landscape changed. AMD fell about 17% in Thursday's market rout, alongside peers.

For investors, the question is whether the selloff is about fundamentals or about valuation and policy risk. AMD's results argue the demand is real, while the share price argues the premium was too high.

Watch for AMD's next guidance and for whether data-centre customers confirm, delay or resize orders after the election.

items.title: Gunman kills a woman at a Citibank campus near Tampa before a guard stops him
items.summary:
A gunman killed a woman at a Citibank office campus near Tampa, Florida, before a security guard shot and stopped him, according to Associated Press reporting carried in emergency-services coverage. The gunman also died, making two dead in total at the office complex.

Details about the relationship between the gunman and the victim, and about a motive, were limited in the initial reporting. The guard's intervention was credited with stopping the attack.

Workplace shootings draw attention to building security and to how quickly an armed guard on site can limit harm, but officials typically caution that early accounts can change as investigators interview witnesses and review video.

Watch for the sheriff's office to release names, a motive, and whether the victim was specifically targeted.

items.title: Republicans press Trump to change course after the midterm rout
items.summary:
Republicans called on President Trump to change course after a midterm drubbing that cost the party both chambers of Congress, according to Reuters reporting on Wednesday and Thursday. The pressure came from inside a party debating how much of the loss was about policy and how much was about the president himself.

Democrats flipped Senate seats in deeply Republican states and gained at least 30 House seats, in a wave tied in exit reporting to anger over the Iran war, tariffs and living costs. Republican strategists noted the party lost ground in almost every county where most votes had been counted.

Trump has so far pointed to his veto as his main leverage and said he expects to get along with Democrats unless they are destructive. That stance leaves Republican lawmakers in the new minority to decide whether to cooperate on selected bills or oppose across the board.

Watch for the House Republican leadership race, and for any early White House moves on tariffs or the war that signal a course change.

items.title: Los Angeles mayor is projected to fall, with council member Nithya Raman ahead
items.summary:
Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass is projected to lose her office, with council member Nithya Raman ahead in the race to become the city's next mayor, according to election coverage on Wednesday. The result would be a major local upset running alongside the national Democratic wave.

Raman's challenge drew on frustration over homelessness, housing costs and city services, issues that have dominated Los Angeles politics for years. Bass, a former member of Congress, had been a prominent national Democrat.

A change in City Hall matters beyond Los Angeles because the city is preparing for major international events and faces large budget and housing pressures. A new mayor would inherit those files immediately.

Watch for the final certified margin, and for Raman's first appointments and budget priorities if the projection holds.

items.title: Voters backed data-centre limits in 44 of 45 community ballots, a new headwind for the AI buildout
items.summary:
Voters backed limits on data centres in 44 of 45 community ballot measures, according to a tally of local results reported this week. The near-sweep shows how local resistance to large data-centre projects has become a national factor in the AI expansion.

Communities have raised concerns about electricity demand, water use, noise and tax incentives for facilities that employ relatively few people once built. Developers argue the projects bring construction jobs, tax revenue and the infrastructure the AI economy needs.

The local results help explain why investors reacted so sharply on Thursday to the prospect of closer scrutiny in Congress as well. If both local ballots and federal politics turn harder, timelines for new capacity could stretch.

Watch for state-level rules on power and water for data centres, and for developers shifting projects toward communities that actively welcome them.

items.title: Inside the Postal Service's sprint to deliver millions of ballots by Tuesday
items.summary:
The U.S. Postal Service took special steps to deliver mail-in ballots for the midterms, including longer hours, extra staffing, special lines in branches, expedited handling, extra deliveries and special pickups, according to Reuters reporting from inside the operation.

Pressure on the agency was unusually high this year. President Trump had ordered USPS to write rules that would bar it from delivering ballots if states did not turn over lists of eligible voters, and the Supreme Court blocked enforcement of those rules in September. In the last two months USPS delivered tens of millions of ballots and a record 4.2 billion pieces of political marketing mail.

Postal workers described starting as early as 4 a.m. in places like Golden, Colorado, to make sure ballots moved on time, while navigating a blizzard of different state rules on postmarks and deadlines. In 2024, about 30% of votes were cast by mail.

Watch for post-election reports on ballot delivery times, especially in the still-uncalled Alaska and Mississippi Senate races where late ballots could matter.

items.title: Democrats won big in Ohio, but experts say that does not make Ohio a blue state
items.summary:
Ohio voters rejected Trump-endorsed Republicans Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy and elected Democrats Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton, who campaigned on making life more affordable. Brown will return to the U.S. Senate and Acton will be the first woman elected governor in Ohio.

Ohio Democrats also won eight of the state's 15 congressional seats, broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House, picked up two Ohio Senate seats, flipped three Republican-held congressional seats, and won attorney general, secretary of state and treasurer, plus two Ohio Supreme Court seats, according to unofficial returns. Brown won 50.1% to 45.2%, and Acton won 52.3% to 44.4%.

Political experts quoted by the Dispatch said the results look more like a referendum on Trump than a permanent realignment. One University of Cincinnati political scientist noted how hard it is to win statewide when a president is deeply underwater in approval.

Watch for whether Democrats can hold these gains in 2028, and how Acton governs with a legislature still shaped by years of Republican control.

items.title: Ohio's congressional map was drawn to favour Republicans. Democrats won a majority of seats anyway
items.summary:
Democrats will control eight of Ohio's 15 congressional seats after flipping three Republican-held districts and defending three incumbents in competitive races, under a map approved in 2025 that was expected to favour Republicans. The victories were part of the statewide wave that sent Amy Acton to the governor's office and returned Sherrod Brown to the Senate.

The map had made reelection harder for Representatives Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman in exchange for protecting Representative Emilia Sykes, yet all three incumbents won. Newcomers Brian Poindexter, Kristina Knickerbocker and Don Leonard defeated Republican Representatives Max Miller, Mike Turner and Mike Carey.

Republican leaders had initially proposed a map that could have produced a 13-2 advantage, but compromised to avoid a ballot referendum and a court fight. A Republican strategist said the flipped seats could revert in 2028 with stronger candidates and a different political mood.

Watch for whether Democrats treat the delegation majority as durable, and for Republican recruitment in the flipped districts.

items.title: DeWine says he won't back stripping Acton's power as she launches her transition
items.summary:
Governor Mike DeWine said he will not back efforts to strip power from Governor-elect Amy Acton before she takes office, as Acton launched her transition this week. The statement matters because Ohio has seen fights in past transitions over lame-duck changes to a governor's authority.

Acton, the former state health director, beat Vivek Ramaswamy 52.3% to 44.4% and will be the first woman elected governor and the first Democrat in the office in 16 years. She now heads into divided government, with Republicans still in charge of the legislature.

DeWine's stance lowers the chance of an immediate institutional fight and puts the focus on policy, including schools, vouchers and affordability, where Acton and legislative Republicans are expected to clash.

Watch for Acton's cabinet picks, and for any lame-duck bills that test DeWine's commitment.

items.title: How Northeast Ohio voted: levies pass, charter limits pass, and the 7th District flips
items.summary:
Northeast Ohio's local results are now clear: Democrat Amy Acton was elected governor and Democrat Sherrod Brown won back a U.S. Senate seat, while Cuyahoga County voters passed two levies and three charter changes. Democrat Brian Poindexter unseated Representative Max Miller in the 7th District with 53%.

In Cuyahoga County, Issue 10, the developmental disabilities levy, passed with nearly 63%, and Issue 11, the health and human services levy, passed with about 60%, adding about $166.50 a year per $100,000 in property value. Charter Issues 12, 13 and 14, which limit some executive powers, also passed, and Democrat Courtney Scheff's win in District 5 leaves County Council with no Republicans.

Akron voters approved housing and police oversight charter amendments, and only about a third of Northeast Ohio school tax increases passed. Results remain unofficial until counties certify them.

Watch for certification, and for how the new charter limits affect county government in practice.

items.title: Browns waive Carsen Ryan a day after promoting him, as Fannin joins the injury report
items.summary:
The Browns waived tight end Carsen Ryan on Thursday afternoon, less than 36 hours after promoting him from the practice squad to the active roster on Wednesday morning. It is the second time this season Cleveland has waived the rookie. Longtime Browns reporter Zac Jackson noted the timing suggests the team needs the roster spot for someone else.

On the same day, Harold Fannin Jr. was added to Thursday's injury report and was limited with a groin injury, the same issue that ended his rookie season and kept him out for much of the offseason. Cutting a tight end while another tight end is limited makes the move harder to read as a simple depth decision.

Possibilities include activating a player from injured reserve, claiming a player off waivers, or making room for a trade before Tuesday's 4 p.m. ET deadline. Cleveland has been linked to several tight ends, and defensive line depth has also been mentioned as a target.

Watch for the corresponding roster move, and for Fannin's and Deshaun Watson's status for Sunday in New Orleans.

items.title: Atkinson says turnovers are the Cavs' fatal flaw after a second straight loss to Oklahoma City
items.summary:
Cavaliers head coach Kenny Atkinson singled out turnovers after Cleveland's 124-116 loss to Oklahoma City on Wednesday, the team's second straight loss to the Thunder. The Cavs never led in the game, finished with 12 turnovers that Oklahoma City turned into 15 points, and gave up 21 fast-break points.

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander led the Thunder with 42 points. Jarrett Allen suffered a knee injury in the first half and never returned, and he is now listed as questionable for Friday's NBA Cup game against Philadelphia, along with Peyton Watson and Tyrese Proctor, while Jaylon Tyson and Nae'Qwan Tomlin are out.

Cleveland has lost three of its last four and sits at 4-4. Atkinson compared the problem to the Atlanta loss, saying the team has to take better care of the ball and execute better, rather than blaming any single player.

Watch for Allen's final status on Friday, and whether Cleveland's ball-handling improves against a 76ers team that arrives on a five-game winning streak.

baby.tip: Day 4 tip — diaper math: by today Benji should be having at least 3–4 wet diapers and several stools a day, and the counts should keep climbing toward 6+ wet diapers by day five or six. Keep the little log going on the fridge or phone; it's the simplest feeding check there is, and it's exactly what his pediatrician's office will ask about. If a full day looks low, that's a call-the-pediatrician question, not a wait-and-see one.
baby.fact: At four days old, Benji can only focus clearly on things about 8 to 12 inches from his face — which is, not coincidentally, about the distance to a parent's face during a feeding. High-contrast patterns and your faces are basically his favourite channel right now.
baby.fun: Tiny mission for Day 4: the first tummy-time minute — a short, supervised session on a firm surface while Benji is awake and calm. One minute counts as a win, and a Moose-supervised (from a polite distance) session counts double.
